claims.text: The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state are governed by its processing-induced microstructure.
High-energy ball milling under argon followed by vacuum spark plasma sintering yields an ultrarefined, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi microstructure.
The ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered microstructure contains few or no nanoscale precipitates or intermetallic phases.
The absence of precipitates and secondary-phase interfaces reduces internal barriers to deformation and therefore lowers hardness and compressive strength.
Fine grain size and reduced defect density favor ductility in the processed CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
High-energy ball milling followed by rapid sintering promotes a nearly homogeneous solid-solution state with very small grains.
Very small grains enhance plasticity through grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed processing route minimizes dislocation accumulation.
Nanoscale precipitates or intermetallic compounds would strengthen CoCrFeNiTi by pinning dislocations.
The lack of secondary-phase strengthening produces a trade-off of improved ductility but reduced hardness and compressive strength.
Ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered CoCrFeNiTi will have higher plasticity and machinability than material processed to encourage precipitate formation.
Ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered CoCrFeNiTi will have moderate or lower hardness and compressive strength than material processed to encourage precipitate formation.

A conventional route such as casting or sintering without high-energy ball milling produces a more heterogeneous CoCrFeNiTi microstructure containing strengthening precipitates or intermetallic phases.
The hypothesis applies to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under compressive testing from room temperature to 600 °C.

contradictions.description: The nominal conventional, non-ball-milled comparator is described in the initial-state field as a simple solid solution, but in the baseline field as a heterogeneous microstructure containing strengthening precipitates and/or intermetallic phases.
